title: Geometric Characteristics of Subproblems in Ising-Machine-Assisted Large Neighborhood Search
abstract: Large-scale quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulations of constrained combinatorial optimization problems often exceed the input-size limit of present Ising machines or suffer from degraded solution quality as the number of binary variables increases. Large neighborhood search (LNS) mitigates this difficulty by sequentially optimizing restricted subproblems, but the structural factors that distinguish subproblems beyond the number of binary variables remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, we examine vehicle routing problems and compare a construction based on the vehicle routes of the current solution, denoted by LNS-K, with a construction based on QUBO variables and constraint relations, denoted by LNS-Q, while controlling the number of binary variables in the subproblems. Under the tested conditions, LNS-K obtained shorter total distances than LNS-Q in the matched-size comparisons, and the position variance, a measure of the spatial spread of the selected customers, decreased during the iterations in LNS-K. These observations suggest that subproblem design for sequential optimization with Ising machines should consider not only subproblem size but also semantic and geometric structures inherited from the current solution.
summary: This paper investigates optimizing complex routing problems using Ising machines via Large Neighborhood Search (LNS). The authors compare two methods for defining subproblems—one based on physical routes and another based on raw QUBO variables. They find that incorporating the semantic structure of the current solution, rather than just matching variable counts, leads to superior optimization trajectories.
main_problem: The study aims to improve large-scale constrained combinatorial optimization problems, such as Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs), by utilizing Ising machines within a Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) framework.
main_result: Subproblem design must consider the semantic and geometric structure inherited from the current solution, not just the number of binary variables. A route-structure based approach (LNS-K) outperformed a QUBO variable-based approach (LNS-Q) under matched-size comparisons.
method: The authors compare two LNS subproblem constructions—one based on physical routes (LNS-K) and one based purely on the mathematical structure of the QUBO variables (LNS-Q)—and test their performance using quantum annealing simulations.
model_or_system: The problem is formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model, $H(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T Q \mathbf{x}$, applied to VRPs. The optimization is performed iteratively on restricted subproblems using Ising machines.
key_observables: Total distance traveled ($D(\mathbf{x})$), Position variance ($V_{pos}$), and the iterative trajectory of solution quality during LNS.
important_parameters: The comparison uses a matched-size protocol, ensuring both LNS variants operate on subproblems with an equal number of binary variables ($B_m$).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation is that while LNS-K shows decreasing position variance (suggesting localization), the authors note this does not prove causality regarding total distance improvement.
figures_summary: Figures compare the iterative evolution of total distance and position variance for LNS-K versus LNS-Q across varying subproblem sizes, showing distinct trajectories.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the challenge of large QUBOs in LNS, details the two competing subproblem constructions (LNS-K vs. LNS-Q), compares their performance on VRP metrics under matched-size conditions, and concludes that structural information is paramount for effective quantum optimization design.
why_interesting: This work bridges combinatorial optimization heuristics with quantum hardware constraints, providing insights into how the *structure* of a problem's representation (semantic vs. purely mathematical) impacts performance on quantum annealers.

(a) Feasible-solution probability obtained with D-Wave Advantage 4.1 for small VRP instances. (b) Normalized total dis- tance obtained with D-Wave Advantage 4.1. (c) Final total distance obtained with Fixstars Amplify AE for VRP instances with 100, 200, 300, and 400 customers. In the naive approach, the full QUBO problem is submitted to the Ising machine once. In LNS, sub- problems are solved...

Fig. 2. Final total distance obtained by LNS-K and LNS-Q for a vehicle routing problem with 400 customers. LNS-K constructs a subproblem from selected vehicles and the customers visited by those vehicles in the current solution, whereas LNS-Q constructs a subproblem from QUBO variables and the associated constraints. The horizontal labels indicate K′ for LNS-K and n′ for LNS-Q. The corresponding numbers of binary variables in the subprob- lems are summarized in Table II. Although n′ allows LNS-Q to control the subproblem size more finely, LNS-K gives shorter final total distances under the tested conditions.

Fig. 3. Iterative behavior of LNS-K and LNS-Q for subproblems with the same number of binary variables. The results are for a vehicle routing prob- lem with 400 customers. Each row corresponds to K′ = 2, 3, 4, and 5 in LNS-K, and n′ in LNS-Q is chosen to match the corresponding subproblem size, as listed in Table II. (a) Total distance of the current solution. LNS-K shows faster iterative improvement than LNS-Q, especially for smaller sub- problems. (b) Position variance of the selected customer set. In LNS-K, the selected customer set becomes more spatially localized during the optimiza- tion, whereas the position variance in LNS-Q remains nearly constant.
